summary: Psalm 40 moves from remembered rescue to public praise: the speaker waited, was lifted from a pit, and now tells the assembly what God has done. The poem then turns from thanksgiving to renewed danger, confession, and urgent appeal for help. It ends with the speaker poor and needy, still calling God his help and deliverer.
whyItMatters: This psalm shows how thanksgiving and lament can stand inside one prayer. In Book I of Psalms, it fits the recurring pattern of a David-associated speaker who remembers rescue while still facing enemies, guilt, and need.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with David, though Psalms as a book is an anthology with many writers and collections, and such headings can mark authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as words for public and private prayer.
context.date: The Psalms preserve material from different periods, from the monarchy through later anthology formation; assigning one date to the whole collection would be misleading.
context.setting: Book I of Psalms, dominated by David-associated prayers of distress and confidence. This chapter speaks from remembered rescue, public assembly, and a present crisis.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, moving through testimony, praise, confession, and petition.

outline.heading: Rescue Remembered
outline.note: The speaker says Yahweh heard his cry, lifted him from a pit, set him securely, and gave him a new song.

outline.heading: Trust And Countless Works
outline.note: The psalm blesses the one who trusts Yahweh and says God's works and thoughts are beyond counting.

outline.heading: Obedience Over Offerings
outline.note: The speaker says sacrifice and offering are not what God desired, and presents himself as one who delights to do God's will.

outline.heading: Public Witness
outline.note: The speaker insists he has not hidden God's righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, loving kindness, or truth from the great assembly.

outline.heading: Mercy In Present Trouble
outline.note: The prayer turns urgent: the speaker asks not to be deprived of mercy because evils and iniquities have overtaken him.

outline.heading: Enemies And Seekers
outline.note: The speaker asks that those seeking his destruction be put to shame, while those who seek God rejoice and exalt Yahweh.

outline.heading: Poor And Needy
outline.note: The psalm closes with a direct plea: the speaker is poor and needy, yet names God as help and deliverer.

keyVerses.text: He brought me up also out of a horrible pit, out of the miry clay. He set my feet on a rock, and gave me a firm place to stand.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the central image of rescue: helplessness replaced by a secure place to stand.

keyVerses.text: Many, Yahweh, my God, are the wonderful works which you have done, and your thoughts which are toward us. They can’t be declared back to you. If I would declare and speak of them, they are more than can be counted.
keyVerses.why: The speaker's personal rescue opens into a wider claim that God's works and purposes are too many to list.

keyVerses.text: I delight to do your will, my God. Yes, your law is within my heart.”
keyVerses.why: This anchors the psalm's movement from ritual language to inward delight in God's will.

keyVerses.text: But I am poor and needy. May the Lord think about me. You are my help and my deliverer. Don’t delay, my God.
keyVerses.why: The closing verse keeps the tension of the chapter: remembered rescue does not remove present need, so the speaker still asks for help.

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin with waiting?
questions.answer: The opening says the speaker waited patiently for Yahweh and that Yahweh turned and heard his cry. The chapter does not explain how long the waiting lasted or what exact crisis caused it. Its focus is on the movement from waiting and crying out to being heard and rescued.

questions.question: What are the “horrible pit” and “miry clay”?
questions.answer: They are images of being trapped, unstable, and unable to stand securely. The next line interprets the rescue by contrast: God sets the speaker's feet on a rock and gives him a firm place to stand. The chapter does not identify the pit as one specific event.

questions.question: What is the “new song”?
questions.answer: The new song is praise that comes after rescue. Verse 3 says God put it in the speaker's mouth, and that many who see it will fear and trust in Yahweh. The song is therefore not only private relief; it becomes public witness.

questions.question: Does verse 6 reject sacrifice altogether?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says God did not desire sacrifice and offering and did not require burnt offering and sin offering in this setting. In the psalm's own movement, the contrast is between ritual offerings and a person whose ears are opened and who delights to do God's will. Readers differ on how broadly to take the statement, so it should not be flattened into a claim that all sacrifice in Israel's worship was meaningless.

questions.question: Who is speaking in verses 7-8?
questions.answer: Within the psalm, the speaker is the same praying voice who has been rescued and now offers himself to do God's will. The heading associates the psalm with David, but headings can signal more than one kind of relationship. Later Christian readers have often connected these verses with Christ, especially because of Hebrews, but that is reception beyond the chapter's immediate voice.

questions.question: What is the “great assembly”?
questions.answer: The phrase points to a gathered community before whom the speaker declares God's righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, loving kindness, and truth. The psalm does not describe the gathering's exact location or ritual setting. It does show that the speaker's rescue is meant to be spoken aloud, not kept hidden.

questions.question: Why does the psalm suddenly mention iniquities after praise?
questions.answer: The shift is part of the chapter's tension. The speaker has remembered rescue and proclaimed praise, but in verse 12 he says evils surround him and his iniquities have overtaken him. The psalm holds thanksgiving, confession, and renewed need together instead of separating them into different prayers.

questions.question: How should readers understand the prayer against enemies in verses 14-15?
questions.answer: The speaker asks that those who seek his life and delight in his hurt be disappointed, confounded, turned back, and shamed. This is a plea addressed to God, not an instruction for the speaker to take revenge. The chapter presents the enemies as real threats, but it does not give enough detail to identify them historically.

questions.question: Why does the psalm end with need instead of full resolution?
questions.answer: The last verse says, “I am poor and needy,” and asks God not to delay. That ending means the earlier rescue is real, but the present trouble is also real. Psalms often allow prayer to end inside ongoing dependence rather than after every problem has been resolved.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that connects the psalm with musical or worship use, though the exact ancient performance setting is not described in the chapter.
Wet, unstable ground used here as an image of danger and helplessness before God gives the speaker a firm place to stand.
The written book mentioned in verse 7, where the speaker says something is written about him.
The gathered group before whom the speaker says he has openly proclaimed God's righteousness, faithfulness, salvation, loving kindness, and truth.
A term used in the psalm for God's preserving care and covenantal mercy, paired with truth in verses 10 and 11.
